content: Favipiravir vs Standard of Care (SOC): 1. Mortality: Based on three studies with a total of 227 participants, the risk ratio for mortality was 1.00 (95% CI: 0.11 to 8.82), indicating no significant difference in mortality between favipiravir and SOC. 2. Requirement for Mechanical Ventilation: From three studies involving 226 participants, the risk ratio was 1.14 (95% CI: 0.44 to 2.93), suggesting no statistically significant difference in the need for mechanical ventilation between the two groups. 3. Hospital Discharge Rates: Two studies with 207 participants reported a risk ratio of 1.00 (95% CI: 0.82 to 1.23), showing no significant difference in discharge rates between favipiravir and SOC. 4. Transfer to Intensive Care Unit (ICU): Two studies with 79 participants yielded a risk ratio of 3.79 (95% CI: 0.47 to 30.55), indicating a wide confidence interval and no definitive conclusion regarding ICU transfer rates. 5. Serious Adverse Events (SAEs): Two studies with 167 participants reported a risk ratio of 0.99 (95% CI: 0.36 to 2.69), showing no significant difference in the occurrence of SAEs between favipiravir and SOC. 6. Time to Clinical Improvement: Three studies with 181 participants reported a mean difference of -2.00 days (95% CI: -3.00 to -0.99), suggesting that favipiravir may reduce the time to clinical improvement compared to SOC. Umifenovir vs Standard of Care (SOC): 1. Mortality: Three studies with 253 participants reported a risk ratio of 0.62 (95% CI: 0.15 to 2.63), indicating no statistically significant difference in mortality between umifenovir and SOC. 2. Requirement for Invasive Mechanical Ventilation: One study with 101 participants reported a risk ratio of 1.19 (95% CI: 0.66 to 2.15), showing no significant difference in the need for invasive mechanical ventilation. 3. Length of Hospital Stay: Two studies with 201 participants reported a mean difference of -1.28 days (95% CI: -2.19 to -0.37), suggesting that umifenovir may slightly reduce the length of hospital stay compared to SOC. 4. Transfer to Intensive Care Unit (ICU): One study with 100 participants reported a risk ratio of 0.05 (95% CI: 0.00 to 0.88), indicating a potential reduction in ICU transfers with umifenovir, though the confidence interval is wide. 5. Serious Adverse Events (SAEs): Two studies with 153 participants did not provide an estimable risk ratio for SAEs, making it difficult to draw conclusions. 6. Time to Clinical Improvement: One study with 101 participants reported a mean difference of 2.00 days (95% CI: 0.27 to 3.73), suggesting that umifenovir may slightly delay clinical improvement compared to SOC. Baloxavir Marboxil vs Standard of Care (SOC): 1. Requirement for Invasive Mechanical Ventilation: One study with 20 participants reported a risk ratio of 3.00 (95% CI: 0.14 to 65.90), indicating a wide confidence interval and no definitive conclusion regarding the need for mechanical ventilation. 2. Transfer to Intensive Care Unit (ICU) by Day 14: One study with 20 participants reported a risk ratio of 3.00 (95% CI: 0.14 to 65.90), again showing a wide confidence interval and no clear conclusion. 3. Time to Clinical Improvement: One study with 20 participants reported a mean difference of -1.00 days (95% CI: -22.40 to 20.40), indicating no significant difference in the time to clinical improvement between baloxavir marboxil and SOC. This summary reflects the statistical findings and their implications for the use of these antiviral agents in the treatment of COVID-19.
